To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the spatial extent of the football athlete’s brain exhibiting reduced FA and increased MD was correlated with the cumulative number of HAEs having translational peak acceleration exceeding 20 g.

the brains of football players who experience subconcussing impacts have more extensive regions of altered brain tissue, and these regions are correlated with the number of impacts that player experienced.
greater exposure to incident HAEs was associated with greater volumes of the brain experiencing changes in FA and MD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the effects of subconcussive brain injury on the brain, and how the effects of subconussive brain injury can be mitigated.
understanding the effects of repetitive head acceleration events on brain health.
the long-term effects of repetitive head trauma on brain function and structure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain is injured with repetitive head acceleration, but the injury is subtle, and the effects of the injury are not immediately apparent.
the brain of the high school American football athlete is more vulnerable to the effects of subconcussive mechanical forces than the brains of their peers.
the brain of the football athlete experiences low-level neurotraumatic injury with each HAE, and that the cumulative exposure to such events produces a greater spatial extent of neural damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
subconcussives HAEs induce neural damage, with greater exposure to HAE producing greater damage.
subconcussively-induced neural damage is not only a function of exposure to HAE events but also a function of the magnitude of those HAEs.
the greater exposure to HAE, the greater extent of brain regions experiencing low-level neurotraumatic injury.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain of an athlete who experiences subconcussive injury may be more susceptible to concussive injury, as well as to the long-term effects of subconcussive injuries.
subconcussively induced brain changes are not only present, but also correlated with the number of head accelerations experienced by athletes.
the brain is not resilient to the mechanical forces associated with repetitive HAEs, and that the brain's vulnerability is not restricted to a single anatomical region, but is widespread.
